title: Picking a project back up after time away
lead: Use this when you are coming back to a project after weeks away, or leaving one you expect to forget. It has two halves: leave a record of what happened, and on return read that record, then check what changed without you.
scenario: A volunteer edits a village newsletter and the website that publishes it. She leaves for three weeks. The example is invented, so every detail in it is too.
input: I am off for three weeks. Close this out so I can pick it up cleanly, and so the new editor does not have to guess.

steps.label: Close out from the ledger
steps.text: The close-out starts by reading a running list of what actually happened this session: commits, decisions, findings noted as they came up. It does not start from what anyone remembers. A summary built from memory leaves out the dull things that later turn out to matter.

steps.label: Decide what goes forward
steps.text: Two changes are done. One was checked by an independent reviewer, but a later edit changed the page after that check. A change moves to review only when the independent check is pinned to the exact version being reviewed, so that one gets a comment and stays where it is. Marking anything finished stays with you. The report is for you to read.

steps.label: The hand-off note
steps.text: A short record: what changed, which decisions were made and why, what is unfinished, and what is waiting on whom.

steps.label: Three weeks pass
steps.text: The note records what happened until you left. It cannot know that the new editor reworded the contact page, or that the hosting plan changed. The next step exists to find those.

steps.label: Read the note, then read the changes
steps.text: On return you read the note first, to get the decisions back. If a memory layer holds earlier decisions, you search it for the ones the note links to. Then you list what changed since the note's date and put each change in one of three groups: matches the note, contradicts it, or is new. The reworded contact page contradicts a decision from last month. You ask the new editor which wording stands, and keep the earlier decision as the starting point until she answers.

steps.label: Close out again
steps.text: Your first session back ends the same way. The ledger now includes the reconciliation, so the next absence starts from a record that already contains this one.

artifact.title: Hand-off and return notes (invented)
lines: Left. Spring issue edited. Contact page layout done and checked. Donations page changed after its check, so the check no longer applies.
Decision. Contact page uses the village hall address only. Reason: the old address was a private house.
Waiting. Photo permissions from two contributors.
On return, matches. Issue layout, photo list.
On return, contradicts. Contact page now shows a second address. Asked the new editor which stands.
On return, new. Hosting plan changed. Nobody has recorded why.

stop: You are done when every change since the note is placed as matching, contradicting or new, each contradiction has an owner and a question, and the first close-out after your return is written. Do not start new work while a contradiction has no owner.
limits: The example is invented, and so is its result. shutdown is a private skill with no public text, and this guide explains the method rather than the skill. A hand-off note is only as good as the record it was built from; if nothing was written down during the work, the close-out has nothing to read. The comparison finds changes. It does not tell you which side is right, and that stays with a person.
